used_for: Logical separation is not informational independence

evidence.excerpt: The ultimate aim of informal logic is normative: i.e. logics that provide us with tools that can be used to evaluate real life arguments and the key elements they contain.
This can be a complex process that must untangle issues that obscure the structure and content of a real-life argument.
EXAMPLE 6: The weather report indicates heavy rain this afternoon, so you should take an umbrella to work.
Verbal inference indicators are a helpful, but not necessary or sufficient, sign of argument.
One issue that frequently arises in standardization is an argument’s dependence on premises and conclusions which are not explicitly stated.
Conclusion: A prison sentence, but not the minor penalties normally associated with misdemeanor convictions, is appropriate.
Arguments with implicit premises or conclusions are recognized in traditional discussions of enthymemes: syllogisms with unstated premises.
Implicit Premise: All people who deserve to be treated as prisoners of war are people who are lawful combatants.
As in the case of verbal arguments, implicit premises and conclusions play a role in visual and multimodal arguments.

EXAMPLE 9: (Visual) Premise: The image [which conveys the message that adding vodka can transform your sleepy night life, as it transforms the quiet village in the image into an exciting urban landscape] Implicit Premise: An exciting urban nightlife is preferable to a quiet night in a village.

So understood, we can critique the argument in poster, for this analysis reveals it as an argument with a dubious visual premise (that vodka can transform your sleepy life into one of urban excitement); a questionable implicit premise (for one might in many ways argue that life in a quiet village is a better life than one in the middle of a bustling metropolis), and an inference which is an instance of the fallacy “Affirming the Consequent”(for there are better ways to secure an exciting nightlife, if that is what one is after).

One principle often used in choosing between alternative interpretations of an implicit argument component is the “Principle of Charity.” It favors an interpretation of an argument which makes the argument as credible as possible.
Standardizing arguments by listing their premises and conclusions is one way to delineate the content of an argument and prepare it for evaluation.
The diagram that follows depicts the relationships between the argument’s key components, using arrows to indicate the inferences it includes.
EXAMPLE 11 When arguments have non-verbal key components, visual and multimodal premises and conclusions can be recognized in a key component table by ostension, or by reproducing them in some way.
The utility of diagramming is already recognized in Whately 1826 and, in the early twentieth century, in Wigmore 1913.
